parsedVerdict.reasoning: The module itself holds together: all four files are NestJS request guards used by controllers (rate limiting, JWT authentication, two-factor JWT authentication and route permissions). That part meets the rule. The problem is a duplicated rule. jwt-auth.guard.ts and jwt-two-factor.guard.ts contain the same handleRequest logic, line for line. Both turn a TokenExpiredError into a ForbiddenException('tokenExpired', StatusCodesList.TokenExpired), and both turn a missing user into an UnauthorizedException. The only difference between the two classes is the strategy name passed to AuthGuard ('jwt-strategy' vs 'jwt-two-factor'). This mapping from token failures to errors should live in one place, such as a shared base class or a factory taking the strategy name. As written, a change to how expired tokens are handled has to be made twice. The rubric treats this as a failure. Separately, permission.guard.ts repeats the same route-matching check (route.path === path && route.method === method) in both checkIfDefaultRoute and checkIfUserHavePermission. That is minor and stays inside one file.

violations.message: JwtTwoFactorGuard.handleRequest copies JwtAuthGuard.handleRequest exactly (TokenExpiredError -> ForbiddenException('tokenExpired', StatusCodesList.TokenExpired); missing user -> UnauthorizedException). The token-failure rule is duplicated instead of living in one shared base guard.

JwtAuthGuard.handleRequest holds the same token-expiry and unauthorized mapping as JwtTwoFactorGuard. Moving it into a shared abstraction parameterized by the strategy name would keep the rule in one place.
